index.title: A Word the Tokenizer Never Saw
index.prompt: A byte-pair encoding tokenizer trained on the words low, lower, newest and widest learned six joins, then meets the word nest, which never appeared in its training text. Which tokens does it turn nest into?
index.answer: n est. Start from n e s t and apply the six joins in the order they were learned. The six joins are e + s → es, es + t → est, l + o → lo, lo + w → low, n + e → ne and ne + w → new. Join 1, e + s, gives n es t. Join 2, es + t, gives n est. Joins 3 and 4 need an l, and join 5 needs an n followed by an e, but the e is now inside est, so nothing else applies. The new word shares its ending with newest and widest and gets the same piece for it.

theory.title: A Word the Tokenizer Never Saw

prompt.p: The byte-pair encoding example on this page learned six joins from the words low, lower, newest and widest. Its tokenizer now meets the word "nest", which never appeared in its training text. Which tokens does it turn "nest" into?

choices.explain: This takes the longest piece of the vocabulary at each step from the left: ne is a piece and nes is not. Byte-pair encoding does not search the vocabulary for long matches. It replays its joins in the order they were learned, and join 1, e + s, comes before join 5, n + e. Join 1 takes the e first, so n and e are never side by side when join 5 is tried.

st is not a piece of the vocabulary. In round 1 the pairs e s and s t tied at 9, but each round joins one pair, and e s won. After that join every s in the training words sits inside es, so s t never appeared again and was never joined.

Start from n e s t and apply the six joins in the order they were learned. Join 1, e + s, gives n es t. Join 2, es + t, gives n est. Joins 3 and 4 need an l, and join 5 needs an n followed by an e, but the e is now inside est, so nothing else applies. The new word shares its ending with newest and widest and gets the same piece for it.

The tokenizer learns no joins after training. It can only use the six it learned, and none of them joins n with est, so nest stays two pieces. Joining a new word until it is one piece would give every new word its own entry, and the vocabulary is fixed before training.

answer.p: Start from n e s t and apply the six joins in the order they were learned. The six joins are e + s → es, es + t → est, l + o → lo, lo + w → low, n + e → ne and ne + w → new. Join 1, e + s, gives n es t. Join 2, es + t, gives n est. Joins 3 and 4 need an l, and join 5 needs an n followed by an e, but the e is now inside est, so nothing else applies. The new word shares its ending with newest and widest and gets the same piece for it.
